translations.text: Barley; cultivation definition and general characteristics

Barley (Hordeum vulgare) is one of the small-seeded cereals that performs well under relatively cool conditions and at higher elevations. Since barley seeds are small and lack the ability to penetrate compacted surface layers, planting depth plays a decisive role in successful establishment.

In cool spring-growing regions with relatively good adaptation, barley generally performs better in lighter soils and holds an advantage in this respect compared to some other cereals. However, in heavy soils, the risk of hard crust formation on the soil surface is greater, and managing it becomes more difficult.
Ideal planting depth and ability to penetrate crusted soil

The ideal planting depth for barley is described as shallow. The reason is that penetration of the barley seedling and vegetative shoot through crusted soils is more difficult for this crop than for other small-seeded cereals. Therefore, maintaining low and uniform depth at planting is an important operational principle.

Additionally, the barley copertile (seed coating) is broader and less resilient; as a result, planting deeper than necessary increases the risk of young stem breakage during emergence to the surface and can reduce the establishment percentage. This point becomes especially significant in soils that tend to form crusts.
University studies indicate that barley cultivation is better performed in lighter soils and at higher elevations. Heavy soils (heavy soils) are unsuitable due to the risk of crust and lodging.

Common planting errors in barley
Planting in heavy soils:

Heavy soils are not a suitable medium for barley due to their greater tendency toward crust formation and the mechanical resistance they create against seedling penetration, and the lodging risk is also higher in these soils.
Soil surface crusting:
Crust formation after heavy rain or irrigation can prevent healthy emergence of the young shoot. Once crust forms, penetration is more difficult for barley than for other small-seeded cereals.
Excessive nitrogen fertilizer:
Abundant nitrogen fertilizer causes lodging and reduces grain quality, especially for malting barley. Nitrogen management during establishment must be carried out carefully.

Limitations in evidence generalizability

The existing evidence is exclusively from a single academic institution focused on United States conditions and pertains to the climate of Wisconsin and the northwestern US. The described planting depth is only interpretable within the framework of those same conditions and lacks generalized validity for Iranian soils, planting calendars, and geographical conditions. The results are valid only within the scope and conditions of that evidence and should not be cited as direct recommendations for Iranian farms.
Source: University of Wisconsin, Barley Section
Barley seed planting depth in light and heavy soils; common errors

Barley planting depth should be shallow; deeper planting increases the risk of young stem breakage. Heavy soils are unsuitable due to the risk of crust and lodging, and excessive nitrogen fertilizer reduces grain quality, especially for malting barley.
What is the ideal planting depth for barley and why should it not be planted deeply?

The ideal planting depth for barley is recommended to be shallow. Penetration through crusted soils is more difficult for barley than for other small-seeded cereals, and barley's copertile is broader and less resilient; as a result, deeper planting increases the risk of young stem breakage.
Can barley be planted in heavy soils?

No. Barley cultivation performs better in lighter soils, and heavy soils are unsuitable due to the risk of crust and lodging. The formation of a hard crust on the soil surface in these textures makes seedling penetration more difficult.
What is the effect of nitrogen fertilizer on barley and what risk does it pose?

Excessive nitrogen fertilizer causes lodging and reduces grain quality; this quality reduction is especially significant for malting barley. Nitrogen management must be such that mechanical stress pressure and grain quality decline are prevented.
